PREFACE 


My first duty in this preface 1s to express my grateful 
thanks to the British Academy and the Syndics of the 
Cambridge University Press for their generous assistance 
in providing for its publication; my next to acknowledge 
my very great indebtedness to Dr R. L. Poole, to whose 
suggestion the work 1s due, and without whose encourage- 
ment and advice it would never have been brought to a 
conclusion. 

The object of the edition is to provide a sound text of 
the Defensor Pacis based on the manuscripts, and it is hoped 
that this remarkable work may thereby be more easily 
studied by scholars than hitherto. In the examination of 
manuscripts I have met with much assistance, for which I 
owe warm thanks: to the President and Fellows of Mag- 
dalen College, Oxford, the Master and Fellows of Gonville 
and Caius College, Cambridge, the Bibliothéque Nationale, 
Paris, for the loan of most valuable manuscripts; to the 
Lord Bishop and the Cathedral Chapter of Tortosa for per- 
mission to obtain photographs of MS. T; to the Hof- 
- bibliothek, Vienna, and the City Library of Bruges, for 
` permission to obtain rotographs of their MSS., as well as 
for most important aid in doing so to Professor H. Pirenne, 
and Professor Paul Bergmans, Librarian of the University 
of Ghent; to Monsieur Charles Porée, archivist of the 
_ Department of Yonne, for much kindness in enabling me 
.. to examine and obtain a photograph of MS. G. Here, too, 


vi PREFACE 


it is a pleasure to record my thanks to the Rev. G. F. 
Jackson, and to Mr James Witty, H. B. M. Vice-Consul

For assistance and criticism in preparing the text I owe

I. MARSILIUS OF PADUA. JOHN OF JANDUN 


ALTHOUGH the Defensor Pacis purports to be the work of a single 
author, Marsilius of Padua, it cannot be doubted from the external 
evidence that a second hand was concerned in it, that of John or 
Jandun'. The latter's share in the actual composition remains 
dubious?; but he was at any rate considered equally responsible with 
Marsilius for the heretical opinions propounded in Dictio II. The 
lives of the two authors have been discussed by Valois and Mr 
C. K. Brampton among others’; and it is only necessary here to 
trace the chief outlines, adding a little more detail on one or two 
points on which I venture to hold a different opinion. 

Marsilio dei Mainardini was a Paduan popolano‘, son to the notary 
to the University of Padua, Bonmatteo. He was probably born be- 
tween 1275 and 1280. After a little hesitation between law and 
medicine he decided on the advice of his friend, the historian 
Albertino Mussato (1262-1329), to qualify in medicine; this 
he did before r311*. He practised for a while at Padua as a

INTRODUCTION xi 


This episode did not last long, however. We hear next of 
incoherent wanderings, perhaps office-seeking!; and then comes a 
resumption of medicine at the side of an “egregius doctor" ?. With 
this I should identify his return to Paris, where we find him 
practising as a physician at the time of the writing of the Defensor 
Pacis. His friendship with John of Jandun was already probably of 
old date, but John was much resident at Senlis and perhaps only 
returned to Paris in 1323?. On 24 June 1324 the Defensor Pacis 
was finished. How long it took for the book and its authors to get 
suspected we hardly know, but early in 1326, two months before 
the authorship was publicly known, Marsilius and John fled to 
Germany to the court of Lewis IV at Nuremberg. They adopted 
perhaps the disguise, or were thought to have adopted the profession, 
of swordsmen, mercenary soldiers*. In any case they were well re- 
ceived, and soon publicly continued their revolutionary propaganda. 
Meantime they were deprived and cited as heretics by Pope John 
(3, 9 April 1327), and then condemned on six main points on 
23 October 1327*. Marsilius accompanied Lewis IV on his Ramer- 
zug* and inspired the revolutionary proceedings at Rome, which ' 
seem a doctrinaire attempt to translate the theories of the Defensor 
into action. He was appointed vicar of the City in spiritualities, and 
persecuted adherents of Pope John. In reward, he is said to have 
been appointed archbishop of Milan in derogation of the claims of 
Giovanni Visconti. If this were so, he never took possession of the 
see, for the Visconti deserted Lewis as he returned to Lombardy 
from the strange Roman coronation.

xii INTRODUCTION 


Little is known of the subsequent life of Marsilius. Lewis refused 
to give him up, and he seems to have lived in Bavaria as a physician 
and counsellor. About 1341-42 he composed the twin works or 
single work of the Defenser Minor and the Tractatus de iurisdictione 
imperatoris in causis matrimonialibus. By 10 April 1343 he was 
known to be dead?. 

'The biography of John of Jandun is briefer, though he was a 
more voluminous author than his friend. Born at Jandun in Cham- 
pagne, he became in the early years of the fourteenth century a 
notable teacher in the faculty of arts in the University of Paris. 
His commentaries on Aristotle show him to have been an Averroist, 
and the scepticism of Christian dogma, which he formally disavows, 
is but thinly disguised. In April 1316 we find him magister artis- 
tarum in the Collége de Navarre recently founded under the will 
of Queen Joan, the wife of Philip the Fair. He, too, gained pro- 
motion from Pope John XXII, who on 13 November 1316 
appointed him to a canonry at Senlis. At Senlis henceforward he 
must have spent much of his time, and it was there that he received 
on 3 July 1323 that pressing invitation from one of his friends, 
whom it is natural to identify with Marsilius, to return to Paris, 
and that he wrote instead the De Laudibus Silvanecti. This tiny work 
aroused indignation at Paris, which John sought to allay by a fellow 
piece, De Laudibus Parisius, finished on 4 November 1323. He was 
then still hoping to write an official pamphlet in favour of the 
*universal monarchy" being vested in the Kings of France. We 
next hear of him at Paris, buying the eventual possession of a house 
for his life on 19 June 1324. Then in 1326 his share in the De- 
fensor Pacis was known, and he fled with Marsilius, whose 
‘condemnations he shared. He was equally important with his 
friend in the singular proceedings of Lewis IV at Rome, and was 
rewarded with the post of councillor and the bishopric of Ferrara?,

II. THE STRUCTURE AND CONTENTS OF THE 
DEFENSOR PACIS 

Tue Defensor Pacis is first and foremost an attempt to destroy what 
its author considers a great abuse: the papal supremacy as conceived 
by such a pope as. Boniface VIII and the whole structure of eccle- 
siastical jurisdiction as set forth in the Canon Law. This abuse, 
he thinks, has done incalculable harm and threatens ruin to civil 
government, causing strife and wrecking its authority ; and he does 
not conceal the fact that it is the condition of Italy, or at least 
the northern half of Italy (Italicum regnum), caused by papal and 
ecclesiastical interference, that has chiefly moved him to write the 
book. This object, however, involved the necessity of proving two 
theses, both singularly revolutionary, not only in regard to the 
positions reached but in the principles by which they were obtained. 
If we except the avowed heretics, followers of other religions, and 
unbelievers, to whom no appeal is made, the West European public 
accepted the papal supremacy and independent ecclesiastical juris- 
diction as of Divine Appointment; and if this were so, of course their 
abolition was against God's Will and against the natural order. It was 
necessary, then, to show that no special Divine Revelation created 
them; and also that the very nature of the “perfecta communitas," 
the State, excluded them as incompatible with its working. Thus 
they could not even be appropriate human inventions for the benefit 
of a Christian society. They would be against nature. Obviously, 
then, the author was embarked on a double research; first, the 
nature, structure, and ideal of the State, ;.e. the community in which 
men live and by which they regulate their mutual relations—this 
being a research into the nature of things; and secondly, what 
government and powers were really laid down by Divine Revela- 
tion for the Christian Church and clergy. The twoobjects of research 
correspond to the main divisions of the book, Dictiones I and II; 
Dictio III merely sums up the conclusions and points the moral. 


1 See the discussion in Valois, of. cit., pp. 600-602, Brampton, Engl. Hist. 


Rev. XXXVII, pp. 511—513.

xiv INTRODUCTION 


In Dictio I, which deals with the natural (and therefore Divinely 
authorized) State (civitas aut regnum), it is curious to see how prac- 
tical this doctrinaire reformer is. He either uses or adapts Aristotle's 
Politics (itself a compendium of Greek experience)—and it must be 
owned that when he merely filters Aristotle he is at his driest and 
least informing!—or he meets practical difficulties with practical 
remedies, and those difficulties are of his time, and those remedies 
especially reflect an actual state of things, the Italian City-states of his 
day. Gone is the quaint academic discussion in St Thomas Aquinas? 
on the choice of a salubrious, fertile, well-wooded, well-watered 
land to rule (not practical politics then for any but a marauding 
Tartar) by the ruler! Gone, too, the belief that an elementary in- 
struction on morality (needful for all persons and occupations) meets 
the special problems of statesmanship. Instead we have a series of 
constitutional and administrative principles and difficulties laid down 
or solved as the case may be; and in spite of their abstract form, 
necessary to the scholastic method and the orientation of the time, 
these principles and difficulties refer, often with considerable detail 
which differentiates them from the alien detail in Aristotle and 
Antiquity seen through him, to actual circumstances before Europe 
in the early fourteenth century and more especially in most tell-tale 
instances to particular problems engaging the Italian City-states and 
nowhere else in Europe. The author, while seldom mentioning and 
even then perhapserasing names, deals with politics in a realistic spirit 
(as a contemporary theologian would sins, but not politics), forming 
his ideal state from a consideration of the actual characteristics, not 
all laudable, of men, and adapting it to human needs with safeguards 
from likely errors?: in short, the ideal for him is the best method of 
getting the best results from the real, not a visionary glass slipper, only 
to be worn with magic aid by a unique predestined foot. The whole 
tone of the discussion resembles that of Machiavelli, who indeed may 
likely have read the Defznsor*, and of the moderns in general. The 
actual instances in support are thechief lack; instead we find apposite

INTRODUCTION xv 


quotations from Aristotle. But whereas, in the Monarchia of the far 
greater Dante, the occasions when he faces hard fact seem like flies 
caught in his imaginative web, in Dictio I of the Defensor they 
make up the substance of the investigation. The glimmer of modern- 
ity, often to be seen elsewhere c. 1300, has suddenly given way 
therein to a transitory daylight. 

The author begins with a definition of political peace and discord 
(I. ii): one is the health of the government or state (regnum)!, when 
all its organs function properly; the other ill-health when their 
action is impeded. Internal peace only, not relations with external 
communities, is thought of. Then comes an account of the growth 
of the political community, taken from Aristotle but supported in- 
ductively from Genesis (I. iii): it is a natural phenomenon. There 
follows (I. iv) the Aristotelian definition of the State (civitas aut 
regnum), as the “perfect self-suficing community, aiming at the 
‘good life’ (vita sufficiens)," in this world only, for the next world 
is expressly excluded. The need for various orders of men (partes 
ciuitatis) is next explained (I. v). All this is an application of Aris- 
totle, but the discussion of one part of the State, the priesthood, 
produces an original position. There is a natural institution of a 
priesthood, pars sacerdotalis, useful to the State, irrespective of the - 
truth of its religion. When the priesthood of the true religion, 
Christianity, is established (I. vi), it occupies the same position from 
the political point of view as the heathen, though it has a different 
office with regard to the next world. An important principle is also 
(I. vii) laid down for a somewhat curious future use: the natural 
State requires men of different natural aptitudes, and Nature duly 
supplies them. We then have the kinds of government after Aristotle 
(I. viii)—a mere copy—and a description of the methods of instituting 
monarchy (I. ix), in which occasion is taken to define and dismiss 
Divine Appointment as an occasional miracle, and to insist signifi- 
cantly on election either of a person or a family as the proper method: 
this the rule of one shares with that of elected collegiate executives. 
Thus the ground is cleared for more original matter: we have the 
State, classes of men, and an executive government postulated. 


! On the conception of the State and the terms used to express it in the 
Defensor Pacis see my note, Engl. Hist. Rev., XXXVIII (1923), p. 18. 


xvi INTRODUCTION 


The first step forward is obtained by the definition of “Law” in 
politics: it means both the science of the just and beneficial, and the 
coercive enactments declaring the same, but liable to omit just and 
contain unjust provisions (I. x). Divine Law, real or false, touching 
the next life, is another matter. Judgments on disputes are necessary 
in the State, and must be given as far as possible by fixed impartial 
rules made beforehand, i.e. human law (I. xi).! But who is the “ /egis- 

lator” of this human law, which can decree to it coercive force? 
Marsilius answers: the assembly of all male adult citizens, or in 


default of unanimity its more weighty part (not necessarily a numeri- 


cal majority) (I. xii). Here is a strange provision for 1320: yet it was 
still a constitutional, if obsolescent, fact in the Italian City-states. 
The obvious objections to this pronounced democracy are met by 
a procedure then normal among these very cities: the appointment 
of a select commission to draft the laws, which then after discussion? 
are to be passed by the assembly, the “‘/egzs/ator” (I. xiii). From the 
Italianate */egis/ater" we come to the Italianate executive govern- 
ment, the pars principans. Capacity and virtue are of course necessary 
to the principans; but also armed force exceeding that of any faction, 
and this force should belong to the office of the pars principans and 
not, before he acquires the office, to the person who fills it (I. xiv). 
This republican provision is alien to the hereditary or elective feudal 
realms north of the Alps, and guards against an Italian danger, the 
growth of tyranny, in which the maintenance of private troops by 
the would-be tyrant was an important factor. We are thus prepared 
to hear (I. xv) thatthe pars principans should beelected by the /egis/ator, 
and preferably without hereditary succession. A further duty which 
is laid on the principans, and is best explained by the practice of the 
Italian City-state, is the supervision to be exercised over professions 
and the like: this is especially needful over the military and ecclesi- 
astical careers, lest they should be overstaffed. Here we have another 
foundation-stone laid for Dictio II, where the characteristics of the 
“natural” State are to be appealed to. In the next chapter (I. xvi) the

INTRODUCTION xvii 


question of the hereditary v. the non-hereditary principans is discussed 
in full, once more in a thoroughly Italianate manner! for on the one 
hand an hereditary monarchy like that of France is not approved, 
and the elective monarchy of the Holy Roman Empire is only men- 
tioned as an unfavourable instance to be explained away, and on the 
other there is a curious reference, later deleted, to the doges of 
Venice, and another to the prestige of the non-native principans, a 
peculiarity only found in Italy. 

There now is brought forward (I. xvii) an all-important character 
of the rightly-formed State, which both deals with a crucial question 
of the day, and provides an essential principle for the argument of 
Dictio II (I. xvii). This is the uniqueness and sovereign authority 
of the supreme pars principans in each State. The pars principans 
may be one man or a council; but its action must be undivided and 
supreme over all causes and persons; all other executive and judicial 
authorities in the State must be strictly subordinate to it without 
exception; here is no room left for independent or outside ecclesi- 
astical jurisdiction, and the author brushes aside the idea of the one 
Christian universal Empire as irrelevant and improbable. For the 
rest, the chapter gives a thorough-going theory to a leading con- 
temporary fact; the consolidation of the kingdoms and City-states 
of West Europe into organized and exclusive States. The following 
chapter (I. xviii) on the correction of the pars principans if it acts 
wrongfully, while practical, has least of all a French colouring. 
Trial and punishment are to be carried out or provided for by the 
legislator? ; small and infrequent offences being winked at for fear 
of disturbing obedience in the citizens. 

We can thus sum up the characteristics of the natural State. It is 
an exclusive community formed for Tò ed £v, vita sufficiens, not for 
mere existence. Its Law is necessary for its being and should be as 
complete in its provisions as reasonably possible. Its government is 


based on the citizen general assembly, its /egis/ator, an active body 


which makes and amends the law (a rapidly developing thing c. 1 300), 


! A further influence of Italian conditions may be seen in Chap. ix, Pt. 5 
(p. 34), where hereditary succession for one or more lives is given as a variant; 
this actually occurred here and there during the growth of the tyrannies.

xviii INTRODUCTION 


enacts taxation, and elects and punishes the supreme executive. That 
supreme executive, pars principans, enforces and applies the law, has 
an armed force, and strictly supervises the individual citizens with- 
out exception. It represents the sovereign legislator!, Its supremacy 
in its State and the freedom of its working are essential for the 
well-being and continuance of the State; but independent of the 
legislator it is not: it is insisted that its action should be regulated 
beforehand by the law as much as possible’, and provision is specially 
made for its punishment in the case of serious delinquency. The 
modern, secular character of this creation has been often stressed: 
how much it owes to certain features, at once the most * modern ” 
and the most “antique,” in contemporary Italian cities, I have en- 
deavoured to show: there should also be noted a certain doctrinaire 
attitude characteristic of the time, which assumes a discoverable 
normfor human institutionsand actions, divergence from whichisnot 
only harmful but utterly wrong and to be abolished. On this ground- 
work, as a necessary order, the reasons for the abolition of existing 
ecclesiastical pretensions are to be based, as piece by piece in Dictio II 
their supposed prescription by Divine Revelation is cut away. 

The régime indicated can only work healthily in peace; it is 
subject to the disease of disorder (I. i, ii, xix). To prevent disorder 
by giving justice and repressing ill-doing and indiscipline is a chief 
function of the pars principans. Hence disorder is in general im- 
mediately due to the inefficiency of the principans ; and to this general 
statement there suitably succeeds the statement of the particular 
cause of the inefficiency of the principans, more especially in the 
Holy Roman Empire, due to the development of papal and eccle- 
siastical power (I. xix). The papacy has trammelled, lamed, and kept 
in abeyance the emperor, the chief executive of the Empire, and 
has interfered disastrously with every subordinate community within 
the Empire. 

Thus by the close of Dictio I we have a working model of the 
“natural” State—really an idealized and simplified form of an 
Italian City-state—an account of its most fatal disease, and an in- 
dictment of the papal supremacy and independent ecclesiastical

INTRODUCTION xix 


jurisdiction as the worst existing cause of that disease. But papal 
supremacy and ecclesiastical jurisdiction were, in current opinion, 
founded on the rock of Revealed Religion. To show that the current 
opinion was a mistake is therefore of necessity the next step; and 
this is undertaken in Dictio II. 

Naturally, the propounder of so revolutionary a thesis was aware 
of his temerity and speaks of the certainty of opposition before he 
gives a sketch of the procedure to be followed (II. i). In the sketch 
it is noticeable that no reference is made to the doctrine of “evangelic 
poverty” (II. xii, xiii, xiv), a sign in my opinion that these chapters, 
like two additional ones on papal claims (II. xxvii, xxviii), were after- 
thoughts, called forth by controversies in progress, and added to and 
somewhat distorting the original plan as the work proceeded. 

The ground is then prepared (II. ii) by a careful definition of 
the words ecclesia, temporale, spirituale, and iudex, iudicium, giving 
and numbering their different meanings’. A sketch is given of the 
arguments for papal supremacy, both scriptural and *quasi-political" 
(II. iii), the refutation of which is reserved in scholastic fashion to 
the close of the Dictio. The true argument then begins. After the 
axiom has been laid down that only Inspired Scripture can inform 
us what Christ did and commanded, it is argued that Christ did not 
claim temporal power in this life, but expressly subjected Himself in 
person and property to the civil power and taught His disciples to 
do the same (II. iv) ; and that the Apostles acted and taught likewise 
(II. v). All temporal power being thus denied them, the real function 
of the priesthood is a declaratory one in the sacrament of penance, 
and the celebration of the Eucharist; excommunication, if inflicted, 
can only be so by act, immediate or by delegates, of the local assembly 
(being Christian), as it implies temporal penalties, the priesthood being 
advisers only (II. vi). The spiritual action of the priest in giving 
absolution is like that of a turnkey in letting a prisoner go (perhaps 
in mistake); his judgment on a penitent is like that of a physician 
on a patient, not coercive or final (II. vii). 

It now becomes necessary to define the function of Divine Law 
(i.e. the injunctions in the New and to a less extent in the Old 


Testament), since the priesthood may not enforce it, and the State 


1 Cf. the similar defining chapters, Dict. I. Chaps. ii, x, and Dict. II. 
Chap. xii. 
: 52 


XX INTRODUCTION 


enforces its own human law only. A limitation, curious to moderns, 
provides the solution. Divine Law, whose “Legislator” is God or 
Christ, deals with both thought and act, but its penalties are only 
exacted by Christ as Judge in the next world; its object is salvation. 
Human law deals only with overt acts, and then only if they concern 
the peace and well-being of the State; its prescriptions may or may 
not coincide with those of Divine Law, and no subject, priest or 
lay, can be exempt (II. viii, ix). The appropriate punishment of 
heresy is in the next world by Divine Law ; in this world it may be 
made a civil crime by the /egis/ater, but this is a purely secular 
proceeding for the temporal benefit of the community (II. x). The 
theme is temporarily closed and a bridge provided to the next 
by an exposition of the evils brought about by the power of the 
clergy (II. xi). 

The next theme, however, has the appearance of an excrescence 
called forth by the publication in December 1322, during the com- 
position of the Defensor Pacis, of Pope John XXII’s bull 4d con- 
ditorem canonum. Pope John, the stout defender of the papal claims 
at their fullest, in this bull and its successor, Cum inter nonnullos 
(November 1324), condemned the Spiritual Franciscan belief in the 
absolute poverty of Christ and in the necessity of absolute poverty 
for the perfect Christian. How the Spiritual Franciscans revolted 
and their general, Michael da Cesena, took refuge with Lewis the 
Bavarian is too long to tell. But in this section of the Defensor the 
Franciscan view is adopted, and the necessity of absolute poverty is 
extended to all the priesthood, all the more gladly as it completely 
rules out the temporal power of the clergy. After a chapter of de- 
finitions (II. xii), it is shown that absolute poverty is legally com- 
patible with the use of objects, and that Christ both commanded and 
practised it (II. xiii). The property in Church endowments remains 
with the donor, whether this be the /egis/ator or a private person: 
this is among the various subtleties the doctrine gives rise to (II. xiv). 

The radical attack on the Papacy now begins. Hitherto, there 
has only been maintained the subjection of the clergy to the civil 
power, their lack of jurisdiction, and finally their incapacity to 
possess property. Now the existence of the Papacy, as a creation of 
Divine Revelation, is impugned. First, it is argued that there is no 
difference in Holy Orders between bishop and priest: the bishop 


b 


em 


INTRODUCTION xxi 


in the primitive Church was merely a priest selected as chief ad- 
ministrator (II. xv). Then we hear that the Apostles were essentially 
equal, and that if St Peter was bishop of Rome, he succeeded 
St Paul ; while all bishops are indifferently successors of the Apostles 
in general (II. xvi). This bares the Papacy of authority, but what is 
to replace both it and the bishops as governors of the Church in a 
manner consonant with the theory of the State in Dictio I? By 
that theory the State (4e. the /egis/ater or its executive deputy 
the principans) should appoint to and control the priesthood. 
But obviously it did not when the Apostles directed the Church 
and the State was heathen. This is admitted for the infant Church, 
but in “communitatibus fidelium iam perfectis" election by the “uni- 
versa eius loci fidelium multitudo" is the rule; and as the perfect 
community is all Christian this “multitudo” melts into the “ /egis/ator 
bumanus?, We thus have the fresh term *Jegislator humanus fidelis” 
to express the citizen assembly in a Christian State which can and 
ought to exercise the State's full jurisdiction over the Christian 
priesthood. When the /egis/ator is infidelis the local fidelis multitudo 
with their head have to arrange as best they can? (IL. xvii). An 
account of the manner in which the Papacy acquired its authority 
in days before Constantine closes this theme (II. xviii). 

But the description of the local church falling under the rule of its 
converted /egis/ator hardly satisfied the unity of the Church nor did it 
meet the existence of General Councils, which seemed necessary to 
maintain united action. So a new section deals with the *conciliar 
theory" of the Defensor. Such a theory was necessary to harmonize 
the conception of the universal Church with the far from universal 
legislator humanus fidelis, i.e. Christianity asareligion with Christianity 
as one among other State institutions; nor was it less necessary in 
practical politics if an appeal was to be made from the Papacy, then 
monarch of the Church, to Christendom as a whole. In fact, history, 
practical needs, and theoretical conceptions pointed the same way.

xxii INTRODUCTION 


It was, too, further necessary for Marsilius to produce a “conciliar 
theory" which should both harmonize with the general theory of 
the government of human societies declared in Dictio I, and rule 
out as irrelevant those councils, “general” or otherwise, held under 
the Papacy and assuming papal supremacy during the Middle Ages. 
Marsilius begins by defining the grounds of belief, and incidentally 
both the competence and the limits of a *general council." Un- 
questioning belief is due only to the plain and literal sense of Holy 
Scripture and its absolutely necessary corollaries, and, where the 
meaning of Scripture is doubtful, tothe interpretation of that meaning 
by a General Council. Other writings are open to criticism and 
private judgment ; and it is to be noted that the decisions of General 
Councils are only to have coercive force in this life if backed by 
the legislator humanus (II. xix). A General Council must consist of 
priests and laymen elected by the different Christian lands and 
communities through their several /egis/atores in a due proportion, 
regarding both numbers and worth; they are to act as experts 
only, and are to be provided for and forced to attend the council 
by their electing /egislatores. The Pope has no power to declare 
doctrine (II. xx). The summoning of the General Council gives rise 
to difficulties. The Pope is ruled out. Marsilius really disbelieves in 
one universal State of Christendom, with /egis/ator and principans 
executive complete; yet it provides the easiest solution. We find 
him speaking of the /egislator humanus fidelis superiore carens, which 
strictly speaking means no more than an independent State with- 
out a suzerain, and such States were at least several in number; and 
once or twice he mentions grudgingly the legislator primus or uni- 
versalis. ‘Those decisions of a General Council which have a universal 
application, on rites, canonizations, holy days, marriage, interdict, 
are to be made coercive by this /egis/ator; nothing but its consent 
and that of the General Council can confer such powers on a single 
bishop. The conferment of benefices again belongs to no bishop, but 
to the /egis/ator ; and the same is the case with degrees and licences 
to teach etc. The general principle is plain, but while Marsilius 
avoids a clash by means of the non-coercive character he attributes 
to his General Council, he blinks the possibility of different coercive 


* Thus no council, at least since the early ones, fulfilled the necessary con- 
ditions for valid rank as a general council. 


INTRODUCTION xxiii 


applications by the /egis/atores by means of relapsing into the most 
casual hints of a universal State alien to his theories, No difficulty 
on the other hand arises from the action of the principans, who is 
always looked on as the executive deputy of its /egis/ator whatever 
the last may be in size or independence (II. xxi). The difficulty of 
common action before and after conciliar decrees remains, and the 
remedy is an advisory chief bishop of Christendom, whose powers 
can be revoked at any time. The different meanings of the terms 
chief bishop and chief church are discussed, and the advisory meaning 
is selected. Such a bishop and church are appointed by the /egis/ator 
on the authority of a General Council. Before, however, the State 
was fidelis a General Council could meet by spontaneous coopera- 
tion; under these circumstances the authority of the Pope grew, 
and then a voluntary respect was fortified by imperial decree, till in 
the weakness of the Empire. it was converted into a monarchy by 
“Divine Right” (II. xxii). As in the three previous cases, this 
exposition of the growth of actual deformity of the Church after 
the demonstration of the intended ideal forms the bridge to the 
next main section of the thesis. 

Hitherto, the chief endeavour has been, whether destructive or 
constructive in method, to explain what ought to be; now comes 
a detailed exposition of the evils actually wrought in the Church 
and Christendom by the papal supremacy. As usual there is first a 
definition of the different meanings of the phrase, plenitudo potestatis, 
in which that papal supremacy had come to be summarized. Then 
follows a summary of the consequent harmful prerogatives: the 
coercive punishment and rule of Christians, the control of the rites 
and offices of religion, the creation of the exemption and privileges 
of the clergy, the suzerainty over the Holy Roman Empire, and 
most of all the power of legislating for Christendom in the shape 
of the Canon Law. Here we see a leading characteristic of the 
Defensor Pacis. Whereas supporters of the Papacy, and even op- 
ponents like Ockham, made principal use of the Canon Law, i.e. 
chiefly, though not wholly, papal decretals, in proving their case, 
Marsilius, far more explicitly than Dante before him, expressly de-

XXIV INTRODUCTION 


clines to consider the Canon Law as of any weight or as providing 
any evidence whatever, and indeed he denounces it as a chief abuse 
contrary to the nature of the State (II. xxiii). Then are described the 
leading ecclesiastical abuses: the disappearance of election, the bad 
appointments, the misuse of endowments, the financial extortions, 
the paralysis of the older orderly hierarchy and discipline caused by 
intense centralization (II. xxiv). There follow the abuses of papal 
secular power. The ancient subjection of the Papacy to the civil 
power is narrated; then the gradual encroachments, the investiture 
strife, and the claim by Boniface VIII and Clement V to supremacy 
over the Empire (II. xxv). This leads up to the controversy between 
John XXII and Lewis IV and the evils and abuses consequent 
thereupon, in which the fate of Italy and the war with the Visconti 
evidently rouse the author most, while like another Frederick II 
he appeals to all Christian princes and peoples to beware lest it be 
inevitably their case (II. xxvi). 

The treatise now turns to calmer themes. A new excrescence 
appears in a fresh set of arguments, for the papal plenitudo potestatis, 
partly overlapping Dictio II, Chap. iii. This must be due to the 
publication while the Defensor was writing of new tracts supporting 
the papal claims (II. xxvii). T'hey are duly refuted in the next 
chapter, in which perhaps the most striking matters are the firm re- 
fusal to admit an allegorical or mystic sense of Scripture as against 
its literal straightforward meaning, and the shrewd historical 
criticism on the Pseudo-Clementine epistles (II. xxviii). 

From this digression or addition, we return to the refutation of 
the arguments in Dictio II, Chap. iii. Scriptural arguments are 
dealt with first (II. xxix); then the more abstract quasi-political, 
on which theme a certain scepticism makes a slight appearance 
(II. xxx). This closes the Dictio. 

The Third Dictio contains chiefly a most important abstract of 
conclusions (III. ii); but closes with a striking and fervid chapter 
(III. iii) summarizing the republican ideal of the Defensor Pacis. The 
Pope falls into the background, and we hear how the frincipans, 
whether one man or a board, should be the sole chief executive of 
the State, governing by laws established by the /egislator, and 
attempting nothing unprescribed by law without the egis/ator’s 
assent, for in the /egis/ator’s express will consists the efficacy! and 


1 Virtus; almost the life, the active vital principle. 


N 


INTRODUCTION XXV 


authority of the principans. This was the doctrine acted on by the 
Italian City-states of 1300. 

In spite of disproportions of length and treatment a distinct 
harmony of conception is evident in the Defensor Pacis. Everything 
is subordinated to the main aim, that of the destruction of papal 
and ecclesiastical power. Had Dictio I been a mere treatise on the 
State, it ought to have contained detailed prescriptions on many 
points of State organization, taxation, and law, which are but barely 
mentioned. What is treated in full all has a special bearing on the 
main theme and Dictio II: thus the derivation of the power of the 
pars principans from election excludes any derivation from an eccle- 
siastical Vicar of God; and the description of the right way of 
“correcting” the principans excludes all ecclesiastical power of de- 
position or excommunication. How the doctrines that the sole right 
of coercive legislation for this world lies only in the people, and that 
the principans must not have beside it any rival executive, are 
necessary for the argument has already been stressed above. The 
control of the priesthood by the natural State supplies a much needed 
ground for the control of the Christian priesthood in person, office, 
and property. Even the philosophic account of the natural aptitudes 
of men provides a means of separating the functions of the priesthood 
under the State from the character Divinely impressed at ordination. 
The Second Dictio needs all these principles and uses them. It is 
a decisive argument against the papal theory that it conflicts with 
them, and a proof of the truth of Marsilius’ own inductions from 
Scripture and of his conciliar theory combined with Erastianism that 
they are compatible with them. 

This is not to say that the Defensor’s architecture is faultless. 
Current controversy caused excrescences as the work proceeded, 
and it may be suspected in view of the perfunctory treatment of 
the Holy Roman Empire, and of the stress laid on Italian conditions, 
that had not Lewis IV been excommunicated the Visconti would 
have played a larger part. It is only a conjecture, but they may 
have been original encouragers of the treatise. 

It is natural to ask whether the precise share of John of Jandun 
can be detected in the composition. A definite answer, if at all 
possible, could only be given after a very thorough comparison of 
his own works with the Defensor Pacis; but it appears to me that 


XXVI INTRODUCTION 


his influence is more pervasive than local. The style of the book 
gives little help: it changes with the theme and the books used. 
When papal bulls are being answered it markedly echoes their 
phrases and indignant rhetoric, and John XXII and Clement V 
are refuted in their own manner; when the Latin Aristotle is 
studied, its mannerisms appear. As John of Jandun was a devout 
Aristotelian of sceptical and Averroistic tendencies, veiled in irony, 
he may come more to the surface in those few passages where 
Aristotelian transcription is more complete, the thought more 
abstract, and the tone sceptical?. 'The main author had a paternal 
affection for his presbyterian system, his erastianism, and a passion- 
ate republicanism, which bursts out in rhetoric even in a passage on 
taxation?. This main author seems to me to be Marsilius of Padua, 
bred in an Italian commune, hating the ecclesiastical powers which 
put it out of gear, and anxious to combine the sharply bounded 
and compact unitary State he loved with a kind of society of 
Christendom guided by its elected advisory General Council.

chiefly by J. A. Sullivan’, by N. Valois, and by Professor

but their cumulative effect is unmistakable. There were evidently

ENTRODUCTION XXIX 


A further subdivision into two sub-classes is, however, possible 
in the French class. One of these is best represented by the Magdalen 
College, Oxford, MS. (Q, Scholz M) and the Vatican MS. (L, 
Scholz V). The other comprises the MSS. at Auxerre (G), Turin 
(N), and Bruges (U), and Bibl. Nat. Lat. 15690 (A), Bibl. Nat. 
Lat. 14503 (C), and Bibl. Nat. Lat. 14619 (D). All of these 
have an interpolation in Dict. I, Cap. i, Part 1 (see below, p. 1), 
consisting of a quotation from St. Augustine’s City of God, which 
was also inserted in the margin of L by a corrector. In Dict. I, 
Cap. i, Pt. 2 (page 2, line 29) they read * Catilina" for “Iugurtha.” 
They also in Dict. I, Cap. xvi, Part 13, omit “ut in Venecie 
ducibus satis apparet." They show further a typical form of Dict. I, 
Cap. xix, Pts. 8-9 (page 105, lines 7-16): 

Huius quamvis secundum veritatem dominii seu coactivae iurisdictionis 
in hunc principem expressio singularis (C, A, singularum) factum (omit et) 
exordium primum sumpsisse videatur ex quodam dicto et dono quod guidem 
dicunt per Constantinum fuisse factum beato Sylvestro Romano pontifici. 
Quod quia donum seu privilegium illud non habet (omit hoc) clare, aut 
quoniam ex post factis expiravit fortasse, vel etiam quia validum existens 
ad reliquos mundi principatus nec ad esse (G corr., eum) qui Romanorum 
in omnibus provinciis illius privilegii seu concessionis se virtus extendit. 

A peculiarity of G, U, A, and C is that they omit the last two 
chapters of the Third Diction, and end with the words *praecludetur 
ingressus." By a slip Mr Sullivan! treated this mutilation as the same 
as that of the Editio Princeps. But the latter includes the second 
chapter of the Third Diction and closes at “praebent ingressum." 
The mutilations therefore are distinct, and indeed the Editio Prin- 
ceps, as I have stated, belongs to the German class. 

The character of the differences between the French and German 
classes seems to me to show that the French text represents an 
earlier recension. The changes in the German text, although not 
as a rule weighty, seem mainly to be genuine revisions, removing 
blunders, making a small advance in thought (as in *neminem... 
cogendo"), rendering the argument a trifle clearer. Even if these 
changes are not due to the author, they represent a later stage of 
the text, not a sporadic growth of error, and it will be seen that 
one of them? (not found in all the class) reads like a hasty thought 
of the author which can be dated.

columns. Fos, 1-171, of which fos. 1-168 contain the Defensor 
Pacis. On fo. 171 r. is the note “anno domini MCCCCXV xx die 
Janua[rii]." The MS. is written in a beautiful book-hand of the 
early fifteenth century, and has most careful corrections by the 
same scribe, only to be distinguished by the colour of the ink. 
Unfortunately the original text has usually been most carefully 
erased. The MS. begins with a table of contents. It does not, how- 
ever, mark the parts of the chapters, although these are accurately 
referred to, both elsewhere in the text and in the conclusions of 
Dictio III, Cap. ii. It is the best MS. of its group, perhaps the 
best of all the MSS. Its close connexion with the original text of 
MS. L is obvious, and Professor Scholz thinks? that it may be a 
fair copy of L. Without denying this possibility, I think it is truer 
to say that L was probably used in correcting it. Some few correc- 
tions in a later hand are negligible. The scribe makes his protest 
in the margin of Dict. I, Cap. xix: “Pulcra licet verba, caveas. 
Latet anguis in herba." 

(L) Vatican MS. 3974. Parchment. Two columns. Fos. 1- 
124. Dated Easter 1401. It belonged to Peter of Prato, Provincial 
Minister of the Friars Minor. Its original text is close to that of Q 
as corrected, but Q has words which it misses out; but it in turn 
has been corrected in the early fifteenth century by another hand 
from another MS. These corrections do not appear in Q. What I 
was able to examine of the text seemed to place it as a little inferior 
to Q. It has a table of contents at the end, and omits to divide or 
number the parts of the chapters. 

(R) Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge, MS. 577 (511). 
Parchment. Fos. 1-144. One column to the page. A prettily written

(O) British Museum, MS. Royal X. A. XV. Parchment. 
Fos. 3-93. One column to the page. Written in an ugly cursive, 
early fifteenth century (?). The text is pretty closely allied to Q, 
but is very careless, and perhaps the scribe purposely reduces pas- 
sages to nonsense. It has no table of contents. For the text it is 
useless, but it has the interest of once belonging to Thomas Gascoygne 
(cb. 1458), who has written annotations!. 


(B) Bibliotheque Nationale, MS. Lat. 15869. Paper. Fos. 
1-68. First fo. lost. Two columns. Written in small cursive, later 
fourteenth century. A poor text with many omissions. From the 
Sorbonne. 


(F) Bibliotheque Nationale, MS. Lat. 1778. Parchment. 
Fos. 194—262. Two columns. Late fourteenth century. Allied to 
B; a poor text. Table of contents at the beginning. 

(K) Vienna, Hofbibliothek. MS. 5369. Paper. Fos. 1-201. 
One column to the page. Cursive, circa 1400. A poor text. Table 
of contents at the beginning. 

(E) Bibliothèque Nationale. MS. Lat. 14620. Parchment. 
Fos. 3-137. Two columns. A handsome manuscript, with a fine 
miniature on fo. 3, fifteenth century. Represents a collation from 
two texts, one resembling C, the other resembling B and F. Possibly, 
as K. Müller thought, copied from D, which has a very similar 
composite text. Belonged to Abbey of St Victor. 


(T) Tortosa Cathedral Chapter, MS. 141?. Parchment. Fos, 
1-99. T'wo columns. First four fos. bookhand, remainder charter- 
hand (? French), first half of fourteenth century. The original text 
is fairly good, related to L and Q, but like G etc. it omits the 
passage on the doges of Venice. It has marked peculiarities of 
spelling, doubling the letters properly single: thus penna (pena), 
subdditi (subditi), confferens (conferens), pattenter (patenter), molle 
(mole), leddet (ledet), votto (voto). In proper names hard “c” is de-

(8) The Second Subdivision. 

(G) Auxerre, Bibliothèque de la Ville, MS. 19. Parchment. 
Fos. 1-110. One column to the page, late fourteenth-century hands, 
which seem to change some four times. The folios (between fo. 107 
and fo. 108) containing from Dict. II, Cap. xxix, Pt. 4 “Quod

l. 9) have been lost. The MS. begins with “Desiderabilis” omitting 
“Omni quippe regno," and ends with “precludetur ingressus" in 
the middle of a page without a stop, evidently never completed. It 
seems to me the ancestor of the other mutilated MSS. Unlike any 
other wholly French MS., it marks and numbers the parts of the 
chapters throughout, but this numeration does not altogether agree 
with that in the best German MSS. It has no table of contents. It 
seems to be a good copy of an indifferent original. Here and there 
the text is disguised by a later corrector. 

(C) Bibliothéque Nationale, MS. Lat. 14503. Parchment. 
Fos. 24-143. Two columns. Early fifteenth century. Begins and 
ends as G. Only occasionally gives the number of a part of a chap- 
ter, but usually marks the part as a paragraph. It was corrected in 
the early sixteenth (?) century, generally for the better, but this 
somewhat disguises its real affinities. It has no table of contents, but 
the corrector has invented titles for the earlier chapters. Belonged 
to the Abbey of St Victor. 

(A) Bibliothéque Nationale, MS. Lat. 15690. Parchment. 
Fos. 18-106. Two columns. Early fifteenth century. It ends as G, 
but inserts as a correction the beginning words, “Omni quippe 
regno." It is very closely related to C, and one must be a copy of 
the other. On the whole, K. Miiller’s opinion that C is the original 
seems best. The text is inferior to G. It has no table of contents. 
Belonged to the Sorbonne.

4-121. Two columns, fifteenth century. The original scribe copied

(U) Bruges, Bibliothéque Publique, MS. 557. Parchment.

without later corrections. Belonged to the Abbey of Dun.

I infer from these notes that the main body of the corrections in 
the MS. are by Prior Philip de Othey of St Jacques of Liége in 
1420, that he took these readings from a MS. lent him by 
Gerard Rondelly, canon of St Lambert of Liége, and that Rondelly’s. 
MS. (itself not a good one) was written in 1416 by Goffinus de 
Momalia, canon of St Denis of Liége.

“French” MSS., due partly to the extreme dislike of orthodox 
scribes for the heretical matter they were copying, makes a genea-

II. The German Group. 


(T) 'Tortosa Cathedral Chapter, MS. 141, as corrected. 
For a description of the MS. in its first form see under the French 
Group, Subdivision (a). It is remarkable for a number of mainly 
contemporary corrections, some in the margin, some over erasures 
in the text, which both perfect the text as a “French” MS. and 
result in converting the MS. from a “French” toa “German” form. 
The question is complicated by the fact that more than one hand 


C2 


XXXVI INTRODUCTION 


is at work in this correcting; and the solution is rendered more 
difficult by my having examined only a photograph and not the 
MS. itself. Some four varieties of hands can be distinguished, which, 
however, do not necessarily proceed from as many different anno- 
tators. First, beside occasional additions clearly put in by the original 
scribe as he wrote the text, there are a certain number of additions 
in a hand, 2a, such as “confessum est” on p. 12, which all render 
the text a more correct “French” one; this hand may well be the 
original scribe writing less formally. Secondly, and more important, 
comes the chief annotator, 2); he uses some variety of letter-forms, 
which may be explained by his having the MS. long by him and 
turning to it again and again, but yet certain peculiarities usually 
re-appear, such as looped “b” and “1,” the ink frequently running 
and filling the loopt. His spelling shows the peculiarities of the 
original scribe. This annotator not only made the text extremely 
correct and much nearer to Q as a “French” MS., but also made 
almost all the additions and changes (mere cancellations cannot well 
be identified) which change the MS. into a “German” one. He 
also added the numbers of the parts, whose position he shifts to 
make room for his marginal additions ; and he seems to have under- 
lined the quotations, for where in Dictio II (pp. 444-85) he 
practically ceases to work on the text the underlining ceases too. 
One of his additions (pp. 248—9), which did not get into the Editio 
Princeps, shows that he or his original was at work in 1329-30, 
for it clearly refers to John xxir's Bull Quia vir reprobus issued 
16 November 1329. A third (?) hand, 2c, makes occasional appear- 
ances, as in the addition to D. II, C. iv, P. 11, cited above (p. xxviii) 
and in a correction to D. II, C. vi, P. 12 (see below, p. 170, note o); 
but this seems to me 2b working with a fresh pen. A fourth, clumsy 
hand, 2d, with a liking for a heavily cusped “7,” is also visible 
(* patrum," p. 24; p. 98, note k; 153, note 7; 189, note h; 190, 
note /; 442, note a; etc.), but his corrections are chiefly the inser-

tion of omitted passages, and, when novelties, did not get into the 
text of the “ German” class as a whole. 

The MS. thus revised was, I think, undoubtedly the exemplar 
from which H was copied ; and it isa curious fact that peculiarities 
by which the Editio Princeps, I, and J, are distinguished as a 
group from H, apart from individual careless errors, are mostly due 
to disregarding marginal corrections of T+. It seems to me there- 
fore to stand very near to the author's fair copy; if its owner and 
chief annotator was not, as I hardly dare to conjecture, Marsilius 
himself, he was surely a friend, who (with perhaps an ally or 
subordinate) both corrected the text and inserted additions with 
the aid of the author's fair copy. It agrees with this theory that a 
MS., of French origin, should be copied by the south German scribe 
of H ; for Marsilius and John of Jandun, as we know, fled from 
France to Bavaria. Curiously enough, Marsilius ex-friend, Francis 
of Venice, was in 1328 accused of having brought a MS. of the 
Defensor to Marsilius in Germany. He may not have been the true 
culprit; but may T be the travelled MS. of the story ?? Tt need not, 
however, on that account be the only * German" MS. which derived 
direct from the author's own copy, though unless the Fribourg MS. 
be such, I do not know of one surviving. That not all T"s altera- 
. tions are improvements is natural enough, if hasty thoughts of the 
author were jotted down on his MS. as well as considered revisions. 
It is a great pity that the corrector or correctors practically ceased 
work from the middle of Dict. IT, Chap. xxviii (see below, p. 444), 
but are not these the most jejune parts of the Defensor and the 
least likely to interest Marsilius himself? 

(H) Vienna, Hofbibliothek, MS. 464, Parchment. Fos. 
1-117. Two columns. Written in two book hands (fos. 1-8, 9-117) 
about the mid fourteenth century. Its origin is evidently in South

MS to T, with T original's defects and T's “German ” additions. The natural 
inference is surely that T itself is the ancestor of the whole “German” group.

Germany as the spellings “prespiter” for “presbyter” and the 
Latinizations *Ludwicus" and *Heinricus" show. A corrector 
has later (fifteenth century?) supplied some of its omissions. The 
parts are numbered. It contains the final verses, and the text is 
very closely allied to that of T as corrected; so closely that one 
must be a copy of the other. But T cannot be a copy of H, for 
(a) it contains the passages missing in H, and does not correspond to 
H's corrector's supplements; (/) it shows none of H's trivial errors, 
nor copies even inadvertently any of H's peculiarities of spelling. 
Further, one would have to suppose an almost miraculous identity 
of the original T with H in all those places where T is uncorrected, 
ie. in almost the whole book, and a careful search of H by T's 
corrector or correctors to make at different times corrections from 
H's text, and that in this process H's errors were always noted and 
avoided. On the other hand the process is simple if H copied, not 
always accurately, though well on the whole, T’s text as corrected. 
The marginal additions, with the exception of one or two chiefly 
of “2d,” go into the text, including even a marginal annotation 
of “2b” (see p. 146; cf. p. 306). On two or three occasions T’s 
peculiar spelling reappears abnormally in H : thus, p. 104, l. 14, 
* dottatur" (for “dotatur”’) ;p.117,1.10,“Chorrinci” for“ Corinthi "; 
as well as trivial slips: p. 117, l. 4, “fomose” for “famose” ; 
p. 475, l. 23, “insti” for “instituere” (which H's corrector sup- 
plies); p. 462, l. 17, “usur” for “usurpat” (which H's corrector 
writes). Then some small mistakes of H are explicable as hasty 
misreadings of ill-written or miswritten forms in T ; e.g. p. 51, l. 10, 
T has“foratur” for “feratur,” and H has “foratur” (2 formatur ”) ; 
other instances may be found on pp. 103, 136, 148, 176, 192, 
245, 278, 415, 453, 464, 472, 488. The original H also leaves 
blanks for the cross-references in Dictio II, Chap. ii, and these are 
supplied from some MS. inferior to Q by the corrector. H is, how- 
ever, more complete than T in having the Table of Contents on the 
first two folios. In the rotograph which I have, one opening, 14 v.— 
15 r., seems to be misplaced and really to follow on 10 r., while the 
real 14v.—157. is missing. The manuscript seems to have belonged 
to a convent at Vienna.

INTRODUCTION XXXIX 


article of Professor Scholz in the Neues Archiv’. He dates it 
at the end of the fourteenth or more probably beginning of the 
fifteenth century. It belonged once to the Guardian of the convent, 
Frederick von Amberg (ob. 1432), who probably brought it from 
Paris and who corrected it throughout. The last folio (159) is 
written in a later hand. It contains the first two lines of the verses, 
but not the last. Whether the last folio was also corrected by 
von Amberg does not appear. On the face of it this MS. is a near 
ally of T and H. It seems just possible that it may be the missing 
parent of the following, but of this there is as yet no evidence. 

(1) Vienna, Hofbibliothek, MS. 809. Parchment. Fos. 1—122. 
Two columns. Written perhaps early fifteenth century. The text 
shows in detail much affinity to that of the Editio Princeps, including 
some interpolations, but is much more careless. Its peculiarities 
would be adequately accounted for, if we suppose it to be copied 
from the MS. from which the Editio Princeps was subsequently 
printed. I can see nothing to prevent that hypothetical MS. being 
transcribed from T, disregarding some of the marginal corrections ; 
but there remains the possibility that it derives from a MS. by 
which T was corrected. I has the Table of Contents on its first 
two folios, and the cross-references in Dict. III, Chap. ii. 

(J) Vienna, Hofbibliothek, MS. 4516. Paper. Fos. 1-87. 
One column to the page. Perhaps c. 1400. This is a sister MS. of 
I and the Editio Princeps, much more correct than I. While it is 
not the source of the Editio Princeps, it stands very near to it; and 
while avoiding Is mistakes it has errors of its own. 


(P) Oxford, Bodleian Library, Canonici Miscellaneous MS. 
188. Paper. Fos. 1-67. Two columns. Written in Italy c. 15002. 
The text is allied to the Editio Princeps, but not so closely as I 
and J. It has the Table of Contents at the beginning. From it the 
Defensor Minor of Marsilius was published by Mr C. K. Brampton. 

(Editio Princeps) Here may be ranged the Editi Princeps of 
Basel in 1522, which was reprinted in 1614, with but few slips, by 
M. Goldast, in Monarchia S. Imperii, Vol. II. pp. 154-312. The 
Editio Princeps evidently follows with great accuracy a good MS.

of the German class. It is distinguished by (a) a few accidental 
omissions of words or lines, () a few non-Marsilian interpolations, 
bare lists of references, evidently some reader's marginal notes, 
(c) by the omission of the chapter-parts, of the cross-references 
to parts in Dict. III, Chap. ii, and of the Third and concluding 
chapter of the Third Dictio. It is possible that this last omission 
may be the work of the editor on account of the strongly demo- 
cratic attitude taken by Marsilius in the omitted chapter. 

There is a translation from the Editio Princeps into English by 
Wyllyam Marshall executed under the patronage of ‘Thomas 
Cromwell, and published by R. Wyer in 1535. It is interesting 
both from the time of its appearance and from its omissions!. 

As to other MSS., (M), Florence, Biblioteca Laurenziana, 
Plut. xuiv, MS xxvi, is a fifteenth-century copy of an Italian 
translation, executed in 1362, ofa French version ; and (S), Bremen, 
Stadtbibliotek, MS. b. 35, is a fourteenth-century summary. Ihave 
used neither for this edition. 

As a result, I should put forward the following tentative 
genealogy of the German MSS.; the Greek letter indicating, as 
with the French, a hypothetical MS.:

INTRODUCTION xli 


Defensor Pacis. The work being finished as the concluding verses 
state on St John Baptist's Day 1324, any changes in, or additions 
to, the original plan during its composition are practically concealed 
from us, but they may be suspected where current controversies 
caused excrescences?. A copy or copies were known in France after 
Marsilius's and John of Jandun's flight, and from this or these the 
two “French” sub-divisions were derived. The passage, which 
after Professor Scholz's refutation of the other arguments of 
Dr. H. Otto? remained to suggest a rehandling of this text after 
1327, really points the other way?. There was no formal “second 
edition"; but the author probably annotated his own copy with 
small improvements or additions, one of which betrays a date as 
late as 1329*. These small changes made their way, either partly 
or wholly through MS. T, into the “German” class which is 
distinguished by them. 

In forming the text I have therefore taken the “German” class 
as representing the revised form, and T (corrected) as its best 
exponent, but the “French” text, represented almost perfectly by 
Q, is none the less genuine, and on occasion owing to sheer careless- 
ness in T gives the only true reading. I have therefore formed the 
text on the consensus of T and Q, allowing the revisions in the 
text, but noting as far as I was able all variants of either MS. in 
the notes. I have also given the variants of the Editio Princeps, 
where that was available to me in facsimile, in Dictio I, and of 
Goldast's reprint for Dictiones II and III. H, also, although it has 
no independent value, is collated in full, since its relation to T is 
important to prove. I have only given rare specimens of other MSS., 
merely to throw light on a few passages, for as a whole they are 
too inaccurate to give authority to the text, and L seemed to add 
little or nothing to Q. 'T'he. variants given from I require further 
explanation ; they are only adduced to show that the special readings 
of the Editio Princeps rested on MS. authority and were not editorial 
emendations. I is full of other variants, not registered here, and all

for the worse. The division and numbering of the Parts of the 
Chapters I have taken from H, for the photographs of T only 
occasionally show the numbers in the margin. The titles of the 
Chapters are taken from the Table of Contents in Q. From the 
same MS. come the cross-references in Dictio IIT, Chap. ii. When 
a variant of Q, T, H, or Editio Princeps and Goldast is not regis- 
tered in the notes, it means that they agree with the text; but from 
time to time their agreement is expressly mentioned for the sake 
of clearness.

CAP. 


I. De intentione summaria tractandorum, et causa intentionis, et 
libri divisione. 

Il. De primis quaesitis in hoc libro, et distinctione ac significatorum 
assignatione huius dictionis regnum. 

III. De origine communitatis civilis. 

IV. De causa finali civitatis, et quaesitorum scibilium, et suarum 
partium distinctione in generali. 

V. De distinctione ac assignatione partium civitatis, et ipsarum 
inexistentiae ac separationis necessitate, propter finem ab 
humana inventione assignari possibilem. 

VI. De finali causa cuiusdam partis civilis, sacerdotalis scilicet, ex 
Dei traditione sive revelatione immediata, impossibili tamen 
humana ratione convinci. 

VII. De reliquis speciebus causarum inexistentiae ac separationis 
partium civitatis, et uniuscuiusque speciei divisione per modos 
duos ad propositum pertinentes. 

VIII. De generibus politiarum sive regiminum, temperato et vitiato, 
et suarum specierum divisione. 

IX. De modis instituendi regalem monarchiam et perfectionis assig- 
natione, de modis quoque instituendi reliqua regimina seu 
politias tam temperatas quam vitiatas. 

X. De distinctione ac assignatione significatorum huius nominis 
ex, et ipsius propriissima et nobis intenta significatione. 

XI. De necessitate lationis legum in propriissima significatione 
sumptarum; et quod nullum principantem quantumcumque 
studiosum aut iustum expediat absque legibus principari. 

XII. De causa legum humanarum effectiva demonstrabili, et de ea 
etiam quae per demonstrationem convinci non potest; quod 
est legis latorem inquirere. Unde etiam apparet, quod elec- 
tione sola praeter alteram confirmationem datur auctoritas 
ei, quod per electionem statuitur. 

XIII. De quibusdam instantiis ad dicta in capitulo praecedenti, et 
ipsarum solutione, ac propositi ampliori manifestatione.

XIV. De qualitatibus seu dispositionibus principantis perfecti, ut

XV. De causa factiva potioris institutionis principatus, unde

XVI. An magis expediat politiae monarcham quemlibet per novam 
electionem singillatim sumere, vel aliquem quendam solum

XVII. De numerali unitate supremi principatus civitatis aut regni, 
et ipsius necessitate; unde etiam apparet unitas numeralis

XVIII. De principantis correptione, et propter quam causam, quali-

XIX. De causis factivis tranquillitatis et intranquillitatis civitatis aut 
regni, et ea quae praeter solitos modos singulariter regna 
conturbat, et de continuatione dictionis primae ad secundam. 


DICFIOTI 


I. De tribus impedimentis sive modis adversandi veritatibus in 
hac dictione contentis, intentione tractandorum, et modo 
procedendi. 

II. De distinctione nominum sive dictionum ex quibus quaesita 
determinanda componuntur. 

III. De oraculis canonicis et aliis quibusdam argumentationibus, 
quibus convinci videtur episcopis sive presbyteris inquan- 
tum huiusmodi principatum coactivum deberi, etiam absque 
legislatoris humani concessione, et Romanorum episcopo 
sive papae talium omnium principatuum supremum. 

IV. De canonicis scripturis, Christi mandatis vel consiliis et exemplis, 
et sanctorum ac approbatorum doctorum Evangelicae Legis 
expositorum. Quibus demonstratur evidenter, Romanum, 
aut quemvis episcopum sive presbyterum, vel clericum 
omnem virtute verborum Scripturae nullum coactivam 
principatum seu iurisdictionem contentiosam, nedum supre- 
mum omnium supra quemquam clericum aut laicum, sibi

XIII. De statu iam dictae paupertatis, quem evangelicam perfectio-

servaverunt. 

XIV. De quibusdaminstantiis ad determinata in capitulo praecedenti 
et ipsarum solutionibus ac confirmatione dictorum in eodem 
capitulo.

xlvi CAPITULA DICTIONUM 


CAP. 
XV. De sacerdotalis officii per essentialem ac accidentalem, separa- 


bilem et inseparabilem auctoritatem divisione, et quod in 
essentiali dignitate quicumque presbyter episcopo non sit 
inferior, sed in accidentali tantummodo. 

XVI. De apostolorum aequalitate in officio sive dignitate quacumque, 
per Christum illis immediate collata. Unde probatur quod 
de successorum omnium aequalitate dictum est capitulo 
praecedenti, et qualiter episcopi omnes indifferenter suc- 
cessores sint apostoli cuiuscumque. 

XVII. Deauctoritate instituendi episcopos et alioscuratos ac reliquos 
ecclesiae ministros quantum ad utramque dignitatem sive 
officium, separabilem sive inseparabilem. 

XVIII. De origine ac statu primo ecclesiae Christianae, et unde 
Romanus episcopus et ecclesia praedictam auctoritatem ac 
super ceteros sibi quendam primatum assumpsit. 

XIX. De praevio quodam propter determinationem auctoritatis et 
primatus jam dicti, cui videlicet dicto vel scripto veritatis 
sit praestanda credulitas atque confessio de necessitate salutis 
aeternae. 

XX. Cuius sit vel fuerit auctoritas diffiniendi seu determinandi 
dubias Scripturae Sacrae sententias. 

XXI. Cuius sit vel fuerit hactenus auctoritas coactiva congregandi 
generale concilium sacerdotum et episcoporum ac reliquorum 
fidelium; cuiusve sit auctoritas in ipso aliquid statuendi quod 
fideles obliget ad poenam aut culpam pro statu praesentis 
saeculi vel venturi; et cuius rursum sit in hoc saeculo statu- 
torum aut diffinitorum in generali concilio quemlibet trans- 
gressorem arcere. Amplius quod nullus episcopus aut sacerdos 
excommunicare potest principem aut populum interdicere 
quemquam; nec ecclesiastica temporalia, beneficia vel deci- 
mas, aut disciplinarum cuiquam conferre licentias; nec officia 
civilia quaequam, nisi iuxta generalis concilii aut humani 
legislatoris vel utriusque determinationem atque concessionem. 

XXII. Qualiter Romanus episcopus et ipsius ecclesia sit ceterarum 
caput et principalior; et propter quam auctoritatem hoc illis 
conveniat. 

XXIII. De modis plenitudinis potestatis, et secundum quem modum 
et ordinem hos sibi assumpserit Romanus episcopus, et sum- 
marie qualiter hiis usus sit et utatur.

suscipiamus cum Aristotele 1 et v Politicae suae, capitulis 2° et 3°, 
civitatem esse velut animatam seu animalem naturam quandam'. 
Nam sicuti animal bene dispositum secundum naturam componitur 
ex quibusdam proportionatis partibus invicem ordinatis, suaque 
s opera sibia mutuo communicantibus et ad totum, sic civitas ex 
quibusdam talibus constituitur cum bene disposita et instituta 
fuerit secundum rationem. Qualis est igitur comparatio animalis 
et suarum partium ad sanitatem, talis videbitur civitatis sive? regni 
et suarum partium ad tranquillitatem. Huius vero illationis fidem 
10 accipere possumus ex eo quod de ipsarum utraque comprehendunt 
omnes. Extimant4 enim sanitatem esse dispositionem animalis 
optimam secundum naturam, sic quoque tranquillitatem disposi- 
tionem optimam civitatis secundum rationem institutae. Sanitas 
autem, ut aiunt peritiores physicorum describentes ipsam, est bona 
15 dispositio animalis, qua potest unaquaeque suarum partium perfecte 
facere operationes convenientes suae naturae; secundum quam 
siquidem analogiam erit tranquillitas bona dispositio civitatis aut 
regni, qua poterit unaquaeque suarum partium facere perfecte 
operationes convenientes sibi secundum rationem et suam institu- 
20 tionem. Et quia bene diffiniens contraria consignificat, erit intran- 
quillitas prava dispositio civitatis aut regni, quemadmodum infirmitas 
animalis, qua impediuntur omnes aut aliquae partes illius? facere 
opera sibi convenientia, simpliciter vel in complemento.

DICTIO CAPITULUM III 9 


CAPITULUM III 
De origine communitatis civilis. 


UONIAM autem tranquillitatem diximus bonam disposi- 

tionem civitatis ad partium opus, oportet consequenter inten- 
dere quid et propter quid sit civitas secundum se, quae sint et quot 
primae partes ipsius, amplius de uniuscuiusque ipsarum convenienti 
opere, adhuc de causiset earum ordine invicem; praeopere? enimsunt 
haec ad tranquillitatis et sui oppositi determinationem perfectam. 

2. Ante tamen quam de civitate illiusque speciebus aut modis 
agamus, quae perfecta communitas est, debemus inducere primo 
civilium communitatum originem suorumque regiminum et modo- 
rum vivendi. Ex quibus tamquam imperfectis? processerunt 
homines ad perfectas communitates, regimina, et modos vivendi in 
eis. Nam ex minus perfectis ad perfectiora semper est naturae atque 
artis suae imitatricis incessus. Nec homines aliter scire arbitrantur 
unumquodque, nisi cum causas illius primas et principia prima cogno- 
verint usque ad elementa. 

3. Secundum hunc itaque modum ingredientes, oportet non 
latere, quod communitates civiles secundum diversas regiones et 
tempora inceperunt ex parvo’, et paulatim suscipientes incremen- 
tum demum perductae sunt ad complementum, sicuti evenire iam 
diximus in omni actione naturae veld artis. Prima namque huma- 
narum et minima combinatio, ex qua etiam aliae provenerunt, fuit 
masculi et feminae, ut dicite philosophorum eximius 1f Po/iticae, 
capitulo 19?, et apparet hoc£ amplius ex ipsius Iconomia®, Ex hac 
nempe propagati sunt homines, qui primo repleverunt domum 
unam?; ex quibus ampliores factae huiusmodi combinationes, 
tanta hominum propagatio facta est, ut eis non suffeceriti domus

De reliquis speciebus causarum inexistentiae ac separationis partium

IIS autem consequens est dicere de reliquis causis officiorum 

seu partium civitatis. Et primum loquemur in causis materi- 

alibus et formalibus, deinde vero inquiremus de ipsarum causa 
movente. Verum quia in rebus quae ab humana mente recipiunt 

5 complementum, materia formae praeexistit in actu, prius loquamur? 
in causa materiali. Et dicemus, quod materia propria officiorum 
diversorum, secundum quod officia nominant habitus animae, sunt 
homines ex ipsorum generatione seu nativitate inclinati ad diversas 
artes seu disciplinas! Cum enim natura non deficiat in necessariis, 
10 de nobilioribus magis sollicita, qualis inter corruptibilia est hominum 
species, ex qua perfecta per diversas artes aut disciplinas oportet, 
tamquam ex materia, constituere civitatem et partes distinctas in 
ipsa necessarias ad vitae sufficientiam consequendam, ut 1v? et vo 
huius ostensum est. Initiavit ipsa circa generationem hominum 
15 distinctionem hanc, quosdam in naturalibus dispositionibus pro- 
ducens aptos et inclinatos ad agriculturam, alios ad militiam, 
reliquos vero ad aliorum artificiorum et disciplinarum genera, 
diversos tamen ad diversas. Nec solum unicum individuum ad 
unius speciei artem vel disciplinam, sed ipsorum plura in eandem» 
20 artificii seu disciplinae speciem inclinavit, veluti sufficientiae neces- 
sitas exigebat. Quosdam ergo genuit aptos prudentiae, quoniam 
ex prudentibus in civitate statui debet iudicialis pars et consiliativa ; 
quosdam vero ad robur et audaciam, quoniam ex talibus conveni- 
enter statuitur militaris. Sic quoque reliquos adaptavit ad opera- 
25 tivorum et speculativorum^ habituum genera, quae sunt ad vivere et 
bene vivere necessaria seu convenientia, ut in omnibus scilicetd 
perficeret de diversitate naturalium inclinationum ad habitus diver-

De generibus politiarum sive regiminum, temperato et vitiata, 
et suarum specierum divisione. 


UONIAM autem in prioribus monstratum est aliqualiter, 
monstrandum tamen certius? institutionem et distinctionem 
partium civitatis ab aliqua movente causa fieri, quam pridem legis- 
latorem diximus; quodque legislator idem has partes statuit, dis- 

5 tinguit, et separat instar animalis naturae, formando scilicet primum 
seu instituendo in civitate partem unam, quam principantem seu 
iudicialem diximus v? huius, per hanc vero reliquas, ut declarabitur 
amplius xv? huius; convenit propterea nobis primum aliquid dicere 
de natura partis illius. Cum enim sit aliarum prima, ut ex sequen- 

1o tibus apparebit, ex ipsius efficientiae manifestatione priori conveni- 
enter> ingrediemur ad manifestationem institutionis et distinctionis 
activae reliquarum partium civitatis. i 

2. Sunt autem principativae partis seu principatuum genera duo, 
unum quidem bene temperatum, reliquum vero vitiatum. Voco 

15 autem bene temperatum genus, cum Aristotele, 111° Politicae, capitulo 
59, in quo dominans principatur ad commune conferens secundum 
voluntatem subditorum, vitiatum vero quod ab hoc deficit. Horum 
rursum generum utrumque dividitur in tres species: primum

1 Pol. 111. 11 (Sus. pp. 189 ff., especially pp. 196-7). ? The restora- 
tion of this passage to its true form from the MSS makes it clear that Mar- 
silius was not a precursor of “one man one vote." Nothing was more 
characteristic of the republics of his day, or more inevitable in political 
thought, than the different weight attached to different classes or kinds of 
men. That the ultimate validity of statute-law should depend on the enact- 
ment of the universitas civium, though it would be drawn up by a commis- 
sion of arbitri or emendatores, was also in conformity with the practice of the 
Italian communes. The ceremonies and solemnities referred to are probably 
imperial, and other, confirmations of good customs.

! The procedure of an Italian commune lies behind this picture of possibi- 
lities, with its perplexed grammar. The citizens are liable to summons to 
council or to military service, the latter either against revolutionaries within 
or the foe without the walls. More especially a select body will be so 
summoned, those who have the requisite leisure; and we may compare the 
various ways by which Florence provided citizen troops, by the company of 
Justice, the gild-militia, and the parish companies, as well as the milites, so as 
not to interfere too severely with commercial life, and also to keep control 
in the hands of the better-off. The quasi-aristocratic bourgeois character of 
Marsilius’ universal suffrage appears clearly enough.

11. Ad propositam tamen nobis redeuntes intentionem, dicamus, 
ex hiis quae dicta sunt iam aliqualiter apparere, quae sit? numeralis 
unitas civitatis aut regni, quoniam haec unitas est ordinis, non 
simpliciter unitas, sed pluralitas aliquorum, quae una dicitur, vel 
qui aliquid unum dicuntur numero, non propter hoc quod unum 
numero sint formaliter per aliquam formam, sed unum numero 
vere dicuntur propterea quod ad unum numero dicuntur, princi- 
patum scilicet, ad quem et propter quem ordinantur et gubernantur^. 
Civitas enim aut regnum non est unorum per formam aliquam 
unicam naturalem, ut compositionis aut commixtionis quoniam 
eius partes seu officia, et harum partium supposita sive partes, sunt 
multa in actu et separata invicem numero formaliter, quoniam loco 
atque subiecto. Unde nec sunt unum per aliquid formaliter in- 
haerens unum, nec pertangens unum aut ea continens velut murus. 
Roma namque cum Maguntia et reliquis communitatibus sunt 
unum regnum seu imperium numero, non aliter tamen nisi quia 
unaquaeque istarum ordinata est per voluntatem ad unum numero 
principatum supremum. Quo etiam quasi modo mundus dicitur 
unus numero, non plures mundi, non quidem propter formam ali- 
quam unicam numeralem formaliter universis entibus inhaerentem, 
sed propter numeralem unitatem primi entis dicuntur omnia entia 
unus mundus numero‘, quoniam entium quodcumque naturaliter 
inclinatur et pendetd ab ente primo. Unde praedicatio, qua omnia 
entia dicuntur unus mundus numero, non est formaliter alicuius 
unitatis? numeralis in eis omnibus, neque alicuius universalis dicti 
secundum unum, sed est pluralitas quorundam dicta unum, quia 
est ad unum et propter unum. Sic quoque unius civitatis aut pro- 
vinciae homines dicuntur una civitas aut regnum, quia volunt unum 
numero principatum. 

12. Nec tamen propter hoc sunt una pars numero civitatis quof 
sunt unum regnum aut una civitas numero, quoniam etsi haec8 
velint unum numero principatum, propter quod dicuntur civitas 
aut regnum unum, quia tamen ad hoc unum numero per diversam 
institutionem activam et passivam referuntur, quae non est aliud 
quam diversum praeceptum eis? a principante traditum, per quod

ments of the world nor to that of the Romans in all its provinces; on that 
account later” the Popes assumed universal jurisdiction under another title.

Et? sequitur in Glossa: Quae autem sunt, a Deo ordinata sunt, id 
est, rationabiliter ab Eo? disposita sunt. Itaque qui resistit vi vel dolo 
potestati, id est bomini habenti potestatem, in biis scilicet quae ad potes- 
tatem pertinent ut in tributo et buiusmodi, Dei ordinationi resistit, id 
est babenti potestatem Dei ordinatione. Non ergo secundum Dei ordina- 
tionem agit. De potestate bona patet, quod eam praefecit Deus ration- 
abiliter de mala etiam videri potest, dum et boni per eam purgantur 
et mali damnantur, et ipsa deterius praecipitatur. Et nota, quod 
nomine potestatis interdum accipitur potestas ipsa quae data est aliquando 
a Deo, aliquando ipse bomo babens potestatem, quod diligens lector 
distinguat. ‘Qui autem’ quasi: qui resistit potestati, Dei ordinationi 
resistit. Hoc autem tam grave est quod qui ei resistunt, ipsi sibi 
acquirunt damnationem. Et ideo non debet quis (id est, non aliquis seu 
nullus) resistere, sed subici. Si tamen illud iubeat quod non debes facere, 
bic same contemne potestatem, timendo potestatem maiorem. Ipsos 
bumanarum rerum gradus adverte. Si quid iusserit curator, numquid 
faciendum este, si contra proconsulem iubeat? Rursus si quid ipse pro- 
consul iubeat, et aliud imperator iubeat, numquid dubitatur illo contempto 
(id est proconsule) 7/7 (id est imperatori) serviendum? Ergo si aliud 
imperator, aliud Deus‘ iubeat, contempto illo, obtemperandum est Deo}. 
Non tamen dixit Augustinus: Si aliud imperator, et aliud episcopus 
seu papa iubeat ; quod tamen dicere debuisset, si papa iurisdictionis 
gradu superior esset. "lamen? voluit Augustinus quod, si praecepit 
imperator aliquid faciendum contra legem salutis aeternae, quae 
Dei praeceptum est immediatum, in hoc imperatori non esse 
obtemperandum ; in quo papae praecipienti secundum hanc Legem, 
scilicet Divinam, (quamvis in hoc saeculo neminem cogere potenti 
neque debenti secundum ipsam)? magis esset obtemperandum quam 
imperatori praecipienti quicquam agendum contrarium Legi Divinae. 
Sed papae praecipienti aliud! secundum suas Decretales inquantum 
huiusmodi nihil obediendum contra imperatoris seu legum suarum 
praeceptum, ut hic aperte liquet et 1x° huius amplius deducetur?.

iudicibus? saeculi, sicut ex dictis apostolorum Petri et Pauli et

convinci potest ex hiis quae dicta sunt xv? et xvir? Primae; nec
