igitur culpis aut retinendis ita operatur sacerdos ecclesiasticus et 
iudicat sicut olim legalis in illis qui contaminati erant lepra, quae

1 The revolutionary character of Marsilius’ doctrine of excommunication 
need not be insisted upon. The right to excommunicate an offender is 
reserved to the lay power or to the General Council (itself as he claims later 
largely lay) representative of all Christendom. The lay power, with Marsilius’ 
usual reference to the actual political facts of his time, is given in two forms: 
the local autonomous territory, and the suzerain state. Thus a Paduan could 
be excommunicated by the universitas fidelium of the city of Padua, or by that 
of the Empire of which Padua formed a part, or finally by a General Council 
conforming to Marsilius’ definition of such (for which see below Dict. 11., 
cap. XX., pts. 2-5, 13). The coercive excommunicatory power of the priest- 
hood is completely ruled out.

a Gold., et dilectiones (omitting dilectationes). ^ H, possumus. 7 
H, seu. 3 Q, priorum. © Q inserts ad. 


! Marsilius aims at furnishing a basis for coercive law and justice in this life 
which shall exclude ecclesiastical jurisdiction. Human acts are either (a) in- 
voluntary or (b) voluntary. The former he implies are no subject for justice 
at all in any form. The latter are divided into immanent, stopping short with 
thought, and £razsient, i.e. proceeding to overt or external action. Both these 
as moral facts will be judged by Christ in the next world. "Transient voluntary 
acts, if they affect others injuriously, are the subject of secular justice in this 
life, for if they are unpunished anarchy results and the state and human society 
decay. The bias towards individual freedom is obvious, especially in the merely 
advisory character, so far as this life is concerned, both of religious (sectae) 
precepts and of arts and sciences (disciplinae).

Note. The distinction (pp. 218 ff.) between dominium as meaning ownership 
protected by law at the owner's demand (potestas vendicandt) and the fact of 
use with an express disclaimer of such dominium, on which the argument of the 
next two chapters rests, while it goes back to the Bull of Nicholas III, Exi 
qui seminat (x4 Aug. 1279, Corp. Iur. Canon. vi., Bk. v., Tit. x11., Cap. 3; see 
below, pp. 224, 228, 237, 241), seems influenced by Ubertino da Casale (see 
below, p. 247, n. 1), who looks on Christ and the apostles as (1) prelates holding 
property as trustees for the poor, and (2) as private perfecti renouncing legal pro- 
prietas and dominium, singly or in common, i.e. the power of enforcing ownership.

Evangelicai Poverty was a dead issue in the sixteenth century; but in the

principle on practical grounds. There is no trace of St. Francis’ bride, the 
lady Poverty.

DICTIO II, CAPITULUM XIV 245 


Christus ad apostolos ait: Er qui mon babet, vendat tunicam suam 
et emat gladium’. Sed qui emit aut vendit aliquid, dominium rei 
vel pretii transfert in alterum. Nullus autem in alterum transfert 
quod prius non habuit. Dominium igitur habuerunt Christus et 
apostoli supradictum. 

3. Deinde ostendo idem ex alio sic: quoniam qui habuit usum 
licitum alicuius rei ab illius dominio iam dicto inseparabilem, ex 
necessitate habuit rei dominium. Sed Christus et apostoli talium 
rerum habuerunt usum ; ergo per necessitatem ipsarum dominium. 
Prima propositio huius deductionis famosa est. Secunda vero pro- 
batur ex eo usu rerum consumptibilium quem Christus et apostoli 
habuerunt. Quoniam vel habuerunt usum rei suae de iure, vel non 
suae de iure. Si usum rei suae de iure, ergo habuerunt simul cum 
usu rei dominium. Si vero rei non suae, aut ergo alienae aut rei 
quae in-nullius bonis erat ante usum eius. Si rei quae in nullius 
bonis erat, cum talis occupanti concedatur de iure; Christus 
autem et apostoli per necessitatem prius aut simul tempore cum 
usu rem occupaverunt; ergo ipsius dominium ante usum vel simul 
cum usu habuerunt. Si vero usus talis fuit in rem alienam, aut 
fuit hoc* concedente domino rei vel non concedente. Si non con- 
cedented, et maxime in usu rem consumente aut alio queme 
dominus de iure prohibuisse praesumitur, talis usus esset illicitus, 
quod nefas esset de Christo aut apostolis dicere. Si vero huiusmodi 
usus rem aliquam consumens fuerit concedente domino, aut igitur 
rei dominus concessit utenti usum solum absque dominio aut usum 
cum dominio simul. Si usum absque dominio, usus fuisset illicitus, 
quoniam ex tali usu privatur dominus dominio rei absque facto 
suo, quod licite seu de iure fieri non potest. Si vero usum cum 
dominio concessit dominus sic utenti, apparet manifeste quod sic 
utens, perfectus existens etiam, simul cum usu per necessitatem 
habuit rei dominium?.

! Marsilius now proceeds to his attack on the papal primacy. First he 
proves in Chapter xv that bishops are merely priests selected to administer 
Church government by human ordinance, practically a presbyterian theory. 
Although in this he appears to be inspired chiefly by St Jerome's Epistle to 
Evangelus, an influence from heretical sects of his own day cannot be excluded. 
Then in Chapter xvi he asserts the equality of the apostles and of the bishops, 
so far as they are their successors. Thus the ground is cut away under the 
foundations of the papal claims.

2. Hanc itaque dictorum apparentem contrarietatem amovere 
temptantes, rememorabimur? primum eorum quae diximus VI? et 
vii? Primae, videlicet alteras esse causas cuiuslibet officiorum civi- 
tatis secundum quod officia nominant habitus animae, alterasque 
ipsorum secundum quod partes sunt civitatis institutae propter suffi- 
cientias habendas ex hiis; quod etiam proportionaliter oportet 
attendere in sacerdotio, quemadmodum in reliquis officiis civitatis!. 
Nam sacerdotii secundum quod animae nominat habitum quendam, 
quem characterem vocant Sacrae Scripturae doctores, causa efficiens 
per se immediata seu per se factor est Deus, hunc imprimens in 
animam, humano tamen quodam praevio ministerio quasi prae- 
parante. Cuius exordium in Nova Lege fuit a Christo. Ipse enim, 
qui verus Deus et verus homo fuit, inquantum humanus sacerdos 
ministerium exhibuit quod subsequentes nunc exhibent sacerdotes ; 
inquantum vero Deus characterem impressit in animas eorum quos 
sacerdotes instituit; quo modo primum? apostolos instituit tamquam 
successores suos immediatos, sicque consequenter reliquos sacerdotes 
omnes, per ministerium tamen apostolorum et reliquorum sibi 
succedentium in hoc officio. Nam apostolis aut reliquis sacer- 
dotibus manum aliis imponentibus et debita verba seu orationes 
ad haec proferentibuse, Christus inquantum Deus hunc habitum 
seu characterem sacerdotalem digne suscipere volentibus imprimit. 

Et similiter opinandum est in reliquorum ordinum collatione, ex 
quibus character aliquis imprimitur in animam suscipientis. Hic

! Thus Marsilius ingeniously separates the public function of the priesthood, 
created and conferred by the State as a necessary part of civilized life, from 
the natural bent of the mind (in the case of the Christian priest miraculous) 
which makes a man take up the priestly employment. He has to explain how 
a divinely instituted priesthood can only function by ordinance of the human 
State, and does so by classing together a natural gift (such as manual skill) 
with the gift conferred by ordination. In the ideas of the time a particular 
natural gift conferred on its possessor no inalienable right to the profession it 
was useful in, or control of its exercise; and Marsilius by his classification 
brings the sacerdotal power under these ideas. i

! The method of Marsilius’ attack on the papal primacy is the most 
remarkable characteristic of this chapter. He seeks to prove that St Peter 
possessed no essential powers by divine ordinance beyond those of the other 
apostles, and that the Pope was in no way specially St Peter's successor ; and 
he proceeds by means of induction from the New Testament of the actual 
practice of the early church, and by a real employment of historical criticism 
on the legend of St Peter. Though this criticism is still elementary in its pro- 
cedure, theattitude here and elsewhere is singularly consistent, not the occasional 
flash of modernity that we see in Dante’s Monarchia. ? Luke xxi. 19.

quando actum hunc exercere debetis, videlicet: Hoc est enim corpus

14. Amplius, propter manuum impositionem Romanus episcopus 
non est aut dici debet singulariter beati Petri successora, quoniam 
Romanum episcopum esse contingit? cui non imposuit manus 
beatus Petrus, nec mediate nec immediate; nec rursum propter 
sedem sive loci determinationem: primum quidem, quia nullus 
apostolorum Lege Divina determinatus fuit omnino ad populum 
aliquem vel locum, nam Matthaei ultimo dictum est omnibus: 
Euntes ergo docete omnes gentes. Amplius, quoniam beatus Petrus 
prius? legitur Antiochiae fuisse quam Romae. Rursum, quoniam 
si Roma fieret inhabitabilis, non propterea periret Petri successio. 
Adhuc, quia Lege Divina convinci non potestd per Christum aut 
apostolorum aliquem vel ipsorum collegium fuisse statutum, epi- 
scopum alicuius determinatae provinciae sive diocesis debere vocari 
vel esse Petri aut alterius apostoli singulariter successorem ceteris- 
que priorem, esto quantumcumque apostolos auctoritate impares 
extitisse; sed ille vel illi magis sunt aliquo modo beati Petri et 
reliquorum apostolorum successores, qui vitae et ipsorum sanctis

Est autem et in hiis tanto evidentior necessitas talium fiendorum 
per legislatorem seu civium universitatem, quanto periculosior 
est error circa personam? in sacerdotali aut altero ecclesiastico 
gradu atque praesidatus officio statuendam, quam circa humanam 
legem aut principaturum secundum ipsam instituendum. Nam 
si ad sacerdotium promoveatur perversus more vel> ignorans aut 
utrimque deficiens, sicque curando et dirigendo fideli populo prae- 
feratur, ex eo periculum imminet populo mortis aeternae atque 
civilium incommodorum plurimorum; mortis aeternae^ siquidem, 
quoniam ipsius est docere atque dirigere in hiis et de hiis quae 
attinent ad necessitatem aeternae salutis. Unde Malachiae 1°: 
Labia sacerdotis custodiunt. scientiam, et legem requirent ex ore eius! ; 
Divinam scilicet, in qua continentur praecepta et prohibita obser- 
vari aut omitti, de quibus transgrediens non excusaretur per ignor- 
antiam aut malitiam sacerdotis. Ideoque discernere debet populus 
qualem sibi praeferat pastorem, eo quod ex ipsius officio unicuique 
commodum aut incommodum atque periculum evenire potest. 
Cuius quidem? discretionis seu cautelae populus fidelis habet et 
rationabiliter habere debet potestatem, aliter namque inconveniens 
hoc evitare non posset.

cum negligens circa se extiterit, negligatur ab illo (Christo scilicet), 
qui eum! misericorditer monet et petit ; ne ambo in foveam cadant, quam 
stultus evitare noluit?. Est ergo vel esse debet in potestate cuiuslibetg 
sibib ministrum poenitentiae convenientem eligere, similiter et

1 I.e. Pseudo-Isidore, where the papal decretals begin with the Epistles of St 
Clement. ? The source is probably Gratian's Decretum, Pt. 1., Dist. VII., 
Cap. 1. ? This application of the University of Orleans to that of Paris, 
witnessed by Marsilius, probably occurred between 1 306 and 1312 or else after 
1320. In 1306 Clement V incorporated the already famous Studium Generale. 
In 1307 new statutes included the organization in four nations with an elected 
rector, like that of Paris, long-coveted. In 1312 Philip the Fair suppressed the 
incorporation, nations, and rector, and safeguarded Paris' monopoly of theology. 
There is a clear reference here to the words of his decree: “Sic profecto tradit 
antiquitas Romanos a Grecis pro sui eruditione ius scriptum et mores ab initio 
recepisse" (Fournier, Statuts... des Univ. frang.,1.1,p.37). The scholars migrated 
to Nevers in 1316. In 1319-20, by the action of John XXII and Philip V, 
the university was restored to Orleans and its privileges.

1 One of the obstacles to Marsilius’ conclusions was the fact that the Canons 
of medieval councils (general or partial) and the papal Decretals were in 
opposition to them. He now proceeds to show that unquestioning belief is 
due only to the statements of Scripture, in their plain sense, and to the inter- 
pretation of dubious texts decreed by General Councils. His argument here 
does not at first depart obviously from the positions in Gratian’s Decretum 
from which he practically starts; but it is completed not only by his rigid 
definition of a General Council in chapter xx, but by the remarkable discus- 
sion of the grounds of belief in Scripture (below, Pts. 8-10), with which may 
be compared Dante’s discussion of the relation of Scripture, the Church, and 
tradition in Monarchia, 11. 3.

Doubtless, however, both reasons were genuine.

1 These bishops are Rigaud (Reginald) Asser, papal nuncio in England, 
made bishop of Winchester by papal provision against the monks’ election and 
the king’s recommendation in 1320, consecrated at St Albans 16 Nov. 1320, 
died 12 April 1325; and Isarn Morlane (al. Tacconi), papal nuncio in Denmark 
and archpriest of Carcassonne, similarly made archbishop of Lund in Denmark 
(Dacia) by Boniface VIII, 11 April 1302, translated to Salerno, 12 June 1310, 
died at Avignon in Sept. 1310. The curious story of Isarn’s spoliation of the 
flocks and herds of his diocese may be due to the fact that, sent as nuncio to 
Denmark over the imprisonment of John Grand, archbishop of Lund, he laid the 
kingdom under interdict in 1299, and in that year according to Petrus Olaus, 
Annales, there was gravis pestilentia pecorum (Langebek, Script. rer. Danic.1. 190). 
The interdict was removed by him in 1303 on his return as archbishop.

second drew its origin from the first. Innocent IIT's decretal Venerabilem (see

1 The coronation of the Emperor by the Pope at Rome goes back to the 
famous coronation of Charlemagne on Christmas Day, 800. Already in the 
ninth century the Pope (John VIII) claimed that he thus conferred the imperial 
dignity. Innocent II insisted on the claim in his painting of the coronation of 
Lothar III, and it gave rise to the controversy on the meaning of the word 
* beneficium” between Adrian IV and Frederick Barbarossa. Innocent III took 
the next step (see preceding note). The announcement of his election by a new 
King of the Romans to the Pope, coupled with a request for the imperial coro- 
nation, was claimed by Boniface VIII to bea request for confirmation. Clement 
V ‘examined’ and ‘confirmed’ Henry VII, who at the time neither acknowledged 
the claim nor protested. Clement V's bull Romani principes (see above, p. 367 
and n. 2), working on the basis of Innocent III’s Venerabilem (see preceding 
note), developed the doctrine of vassalage and confirmation fullv, with the further 
corollary that the oath taken to the Pope by the King of the Romans, as well as 
the special oath obtained by Boniface VIII from Albert I, was an oath of feudal 
vassalage. ? Boniface VIII acted on this claim with regard to Albert I. See

1 This is an anticipation (as the use of the future tense shows, in almost all MSS., 
including those on which this edition rests, but corrupted in Goldast) of the con- 
demnation of Lewis IV as fautor haereticorum on 3 April 1327 and as a heretic 
on 23 Oct. 1327. The results of such a condemnation and the possible crusade 
against him were well known from the similar condemnations and proceedings 
against Matteo Visconti and his sons in 1322-3, and against Frederick of Monte- 
feltro and the Recanatese in 1321-2. Among other documents Marsilius would 
know the papal condemnation of Lewis IV's envoys in Lombardy on 12 April 
1323 which was circulated widely (MGH. Const. v. 711 ff.). See also the inquisitors’ 
condemnation of the envoys (bid. 712), where Galeazzo and his brothers are 
termed ''rebelles sancte matris ecclesie...iudicati heretici manifesti ac expositi a 
fidelibus capiendi.” The confiscation of the goods of heretics was laid down by 
Innocent III in Vergentis in senium (Corp. Iur. Canon., Decr. Greg. IX, Bk v., Tit. 
VII., cap. 10). But Marsilius probably had before him the far-reaching bull of 
Clement V, on 27 March 1309, condemning the Venetians for their attempt to 
annex the papal fief of Ferrara. Itisin this that the remarkableslavery clause occurs, 
and there is a distinct echo of the bull’s style in Marsilius. The most important 
passage is given in Eitel, A., Der Kirchenstaat unter Klemens V, p. 189: “Ne ipsorum 
temeritas transeat praesumptoribus in exemplum, bona ipsorum mobilia et immobilia 
de ipsorum (sic) fratrum consilio confiscamus et personas ipsorum, ducis, consiliariorum, 
et aliorum Venetorum, exponimus fidelibus, ut capientium fiant servi, et bona eorum 
mobilia concedimus quibuscumque fidelibus occupanda." An imperfect text of the 
whole bull is in Lünig, J. C., Codex Italiae dipl., 1v. cc. 1589 ff. See above,

1 Cf. Machiavelli, IZ Principe, xxvi: **L'Italia...battuta, spogliata, lacera, 
corsa." 2 1 Tim.v.8. — ? Chapters XXVII and XXVIII begin the final chapters 
of refutation of opponents, being occupied with the arguments for (xxvit) the 
papal plenitudo potestatis, and their confutation (xxvii). They thus hold the same 
relation to Chapters XV-XXVI, as Chapter XIV to Chapter XIII on summa et meritoria 
paupertas. But the arrangement is here more awkward as Chapters XXVII, XXVIII 
partly overlap, partly supplement, and partly anticipate, Chapters 111 (the papal 
view) and xxix, Xxx (its confutation). The reason for these excrescences no 
doubt is that both “ Poverty” and the « P/enztudo potestatis" were already cur- 
rent controversies which were calling forth a succession of tractates in 1320-30. 
That of the « P/enitudo potestatis” had been revived by the views of the Parisian 
master, John de Pouilly, who, championing the parish priests in an attack on 
Franciscan privileges over the right of hearing confessions, had to a small extent 
anticipated Marsilius' views on this point. So Marsilius is here dealing with argu- 
ments such as those advanced by Herveus Natalis (Hervé de Nedellec), ob. 1323, the 
General of the Dominicans, who in his De Potestate Papae was controverting 
John de Pouilly. John XXII denounced de Pouilly’s views in the bull Vas 
electionis doctor (Corp. Iur. Canon., Extrav. Commun., Bk iii., Tit. V., cap. 2), 24 


July 1321.

1 It may be noticed that this objectioń (see above, p. 427) assumes the unity 
of Christendom under the Emperor, just as in Dante’s Monarchia. But the 
argument is that of an opponent. Marsilius meets it without an explicit denial; 
but refers first to Dict. I., cap. XVII., where only the unity of a single state (not 
that of the Empire of Christendom) is in question, and secondly urges that the 
unity of the pars principans (whether of the world-empire or of the single state 
being left undetermined) is of purely human institution, thus turning his back 
once more on medieval theory. In part 15 below (p. 446, l. 15) he definitely 
repudiates the universal empire, and treats the pars principans as a unity only 
secundum provincias.

DICTIO II, CAPITULUM XXIX 469 


Decretales inquantum huiusmodi leges divinae aut humanae, sed 
narrationes aut documenta et in pluribus oligarchica quaedam 
statuta. Propter quod talium ordinatores? contra formam et praeter 
auctoritatem iam dictam, ad ipsorum quoque observationem quem- 
quam inducentes verbis subreptitiis, quasi cogentes comminando 
simplicibus eorum transgressoribus damnationem aeternam, aut 
blasphemias sive anathemata vel alias maledictiones inferentes in 
quemquam verbo vel scripto, corporaliter sunt extremo puniendi 
supplicio tamquam conspiratores et civilis schismatis concitatores. 
Est enim haec gravissima species criminis laesae maiestatis; quo- 
niam in principatum directe committitur, ad eius, etiam supremi, 
pluralitatem et consequenter per necessitatem ad? solutionem cuius- 
libet politiae perducens!.

OCABITUR autem tractatus iste Defensor Pacis, quoniam 
V in ipso tractantur et explicantur praecipuae causae quibus 
conservatur et extat civilis pax sive tranquillitas et haee etiam 
propter quas oppositaf lis oritur, prohibetur, et tollitur. Per ipsum 
ro enim scitur auctoritas, causa, et concordantia Divinarum et hu- 
manarum Legum et coactivi cuiuslibet principatus, quaeh regulae 
sunt actuum humanorum, in quorum convenienti mensura non 
impedita pax seu tranquillitas civilis consistit. 
Amplius, per ipsum comprehendere potest tam principans quam 
15 Subiectum quae sunt elementa prima civilitatis cuiuslibet, quid 
observare oporteat propter conservationem pacis et propriae liber- 
tatis. Primus namque civis vel civilis regiminis pars, principans 
scilicet, sit! unicus homo vel plures, comprehendet per eas quae in 
hoc libro scriptae sunt humanae veritates atque divinae, soli sibi 
20 convenire auctoritatem praecipiendi subiectae multitudini com- 
muniter aut divisim; et unumquemque arcere, si expediat, secun- 
dum positas leges, et nil praeter has, arduum praesertim, agere 
absque multitudinis subiectae seu legislatoris consensu ; nec iniuriak 
provocandam esse multitudinem seu legislatorem, quoniam in 
25 ipsius expressa voluntate consistit virtus et auctoritas principatus. 
Subiecta vero multitudo et ipsius singulum quodlibet ex hoc libro 
addiscere potest, qualem aut quales instituere oporteat! princi- 
pantes; et quoniam solius principantis partis praeceptis velut co-
